parts.note: something distant is far away
the Med is short for the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A farmer has ploughed a field beside some faraway sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Ploughing is one example of working land as a farmer does, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Less than the total amount put paid to Davy Crockett

indicators.note: less than the whole of the phrase means only a run of letters inside these two words is taken

explanation.surface: Something short of the full sum finished off the frontiersman Davy Crockett.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across the join of 'total amount'; 'Less than the' says only part of the phrase is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The frontier hero Davy Crockett died defending the Texan mission fort in 1836 when it fell to Mexican troops.

clue.text: Jury, in nautical combinations, get moving

explanation.surface: A sailor talks of a jury being made to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: In sailing terms a jury mast or jury rig is a temporary stand-in; to make shift is an old phrase for bestirring oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: A jury mast is a temporary improvised one, so jury means stop-gap; and to make shift once meant to bestir oneself and get going.

parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing verb completes a line from Milton's poem L'Allegro, before the closing s

explanation.surface: A line of Milton's poetry with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in L'Allegro runs 'Sport that wrinkled Care derides, And Laughter holding both his sides'; the gap plus the printed s makes the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem, merry sport mocks and scorns gloomy Care, which is the verb that fills the gap.

clue.text: Strong man reformed law in the beginning

indicators.note: in tells us the reworked word sits within the word for the beginning

parts.note: the beginning is the start

indicators.note: reformed means the word law is formed again in a new order

explanation.surface: A powerful man has reformed the law right from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong man' is a noun here, a sturdy loyal supporter; 'reformed' is the anagram signal and 'in' the container signal, around 'the beginning'.
explanation.definitionFit: A loyal, sturdy supporter is called a stalwart, a noun for a strong dependable person.

parts.note: read four-sided as square and understanding as what one stands on, a leg; the sporting judge is a cricket official

explanation.surface: A sports official whose grasp of things is rather old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the second umpire stands at square leg, level with the batsman; 'understanding' splits as under-standing, the leg one stands on, and four-sided gives square.
explanation.definitionFit: This cricket official stands at the fielding position level with the batsman, square to the pitch on the leg side.

clue.text: What Richard would do for a horse !

definitions.text: What Richard would do for a horse !

parts.words: What Richard would do for a horse !
parts.note: recalls Shakespeare's Richard III crying 'My kingdom for a horse!', offering to give up his throne

explanation.surface: A question of what a king would trade for a mount.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard III's line 'A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!' offers his kingdom, which is to give up the throne.
explanation.definitionFit: To give up a throne formally is to renounce it, which Richard offers to do in exchange for a mount.

indicators.note: adrift means loose and out of place, so the letters of A-wing wander into a new order

explanation.surface: Part of a building or aircraft has come loose in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adrift' rearranges the five letters of A-WING. The town is in Greater Manchester now but historically in Lancashire, a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition names a place found in the north-west English county, and this town is one such place.

parts.note: rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane
worker ants are the classic crossword workers

explanation.surface: Someone browbeats the people in a factory with drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cows' looks like a verb meaning intimidates, but it is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle chew the cud, so they belong to the class of cud-chewing animals.

clue.text: " Support the Soil " the theme of this music?

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
the ground is the soil

explanation.surface: A slogan backing farmers is the subject of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer goes before music to give the quiet music played behind a film or in a shop, so it is the 'theme' of such music.
explanation.definitionFit: Unobtrusive music played behind other activity is called by this word plus music.

clue.text: Snakes and ladders, or hares and rabbits

explanation.surface: Board play beside wild animals in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: Snakes and ladders is a children's board game; hares and rabbits are hunted animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Snakes and ladders is a board pastime played for fun; hares and rabbits are animals hunted for sport and food.

clue.text: Think, son, when fuddled in drink

indicators.note: in places the jumbled word inside the word for drink

parts.note: cider is an alcoholic drink made from apples

indicators.note: fuddled means confused by drink, so the letters of son are muddled

explanation.surface: A father urges his son to reflect when he is muddled by alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drink' looks like where the thinker is, but it supplies the container; 'when fuddled' is the anagram signal and 'in' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder or reflect is a synonym for the verb think.

clue.text: That French number is a bit doggy

parts.note: ça is French for that
nine is a number

explanation.surface: A French number has a slightly dog-like quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to dogs is the meaning of both words, an adjective synonym.

explanation.surface: A man named Munro owns a pet monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: H. H. Munro wrote short stories under this pen name, which is also a South American monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer Hector Hugh Munro used this pen name; it is also a long-tailed monkey of South America.

parts.note: a street-corner speaker standing on a box stirs up a crowd, and stirring is also what one does to soap suds

explanation.surface: What a street-corner speaker produces in the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Soap-box speakers stir up crowds into a state of unrest, and stirring soap also churns it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Public unrest and campaigning stirred up by speeches, and also the act of churning a liquid, both carry this name.

parts.note: action here is a lawsuit, so the man is a party to a court case

explanation.surface: A description of an energetic doer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of action' suggests a hero; but an action is a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A party who brings or defends a lawsuit is involved in a legal action.

clue.text: Erratic golfer can get some birdie

indicators.note: erratic means wandering and irregular, so the letters of golfer and can are scattered

explanation.surface: An unreliable golfer can still score a birdie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erratic' rearranges GOLFER + CAN. A birdie in golf is one under par, but here it is a little bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A large Arctic falcon is one example of a bird.

clue.text: An attack by Billy when up against it

parts.note: a billy goat attacks by ramming with its head

explanation.surface: A goat charges someone who is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy is a billy goat; 'up against it' sounds like in trouble but here means touching it.
explanation.definitionFit: Touching or bordering on something means pressed right against it.

clue.text: For the sailor's bits — or the troubadour's pieces ?

explanation.surface: A container for a sailor's kit or a singer's songs.
explanation.walkthrough: A sailor keeps small kit in such a bag; a troubadour's pieces are songs, ditties, which this would also hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors keep needles and small odds and ends in this pouch; read literally it is a sack for a minstrel's songs.

parts.note: a Shakespeare quotation with a word missing and a gap for the speaker; the answer is the missing word then who says it

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare dismissing a meddler.
explanation.walkthrough: The Danish prince says this over the body of Polonius, whom he has just stabbed through a curtain; the first gap is the missing adjective, the second the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish prince calls the dead Polonius a hasty, intruding fool in Act 3 of Shakespeare's play.

parts.note: a vest is a British undershirt

explanation.surface: Advice to stash your cash in your undershirt.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a vest is an undershirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: To place funds in a venture is to commit money for a return.

explanation.surface: Weighing scales showing a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: The zodiac sign is the Scales; the Latin word for a pound weight is why pound is abbreviated lb.
explanation.definitionFit: The zodiac sign is represented by scales; the Roman pound weight gives the abbreviation lb.

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit from China.
explanation.definitionFit: The standard Chinese language and an old Chinese official both take this name, as does a small citrus orange.

parts.note: not a bullfighting arena but the circle round the bull on a dartboard or target

explanation.surface: A question about a bullfighting arena.
explanation.walkthrough: The bull is the centre of a target; the ring just outside it has its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: On a target or dartboard the band round the bull's-eye is the ring closest to the centre.

explanation.surface: A local branch of a club and its member.
explanation.definitionFit: A large bough of a tree and an arm or leg of the body both carry this name.

clue.text: I ride to the trail of the rainbow

parts.note: a scent is the trail an animal leaves for hounds to follow

explanation.surface: A rider sets out to follow the rainbow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ride to the trail' suggests hunting with hounds, where the scent is the trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Shimmering with changing colours, as the rainbow does, is the meaning.

clue.text: Snarl, having broken the net with fish

indicators.note: a broken net is a damaged one, so its three letters are rearranged

parts.note: to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: An angry fisherman growls after a fish tears through his net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having broken' turns NET into ENT; 'the' and 'with' are links. 'Snarl' is a verb meaning tangle, not a growl.
explanation.definitionFit: To snarl a line or rope is to tangle it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Fish eats doctor? What a waste !

indicators.note: eats means the fish takes the doctor inside itself

parts.note: tuna is a fish

explanation.surface: A fish devouring a doctor would be a sad loss.
explanation.walkthrough: The text as held read 'cats' for 'eats'. 'What a waste!' sounds like dismay but describes a barren Arctic plain.
explanation.definitionFit: A treeless frozen Arctic plain is a wasteland, an empty expanse.
